en: Oṃ. Salutation to that Brahman which is Truth. The *Yamasmṛti*.
The Dharma proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti for the social classes in their proper order.
Questioned by the seers, Yama, the leader of sages, spoke.
I shall now declare the expiation for one who, while eating, should touch an impure person, a Caṇḍāla, or an outcast, whether out of anger or even through ignorance.
A Brahmin shall perform this for six nights or three nights respectively;
having bathed at the three daily sessions, he becomes pure through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If, while eating, the anus of a Brahmin should ever leak,
one should prescribe purification for him in that state of being defiled by food remnants and impurity.
Having first performed purification, the twice-born man should afterwards touch water;
having fasted for a day and night, he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow.
If one urinates while holding [the breath] or after having eaten, or if urination has occurred [while eating],
one should fast for a day and night and offer oblations of clarified butter.
If at any time during a meal a Brahmin should become impure,
he should place that morsel on the ground, bathe, and thereby attain purification.
Having consumed that morsel, one is purified by fasting;
and having eaten all of it, one is purified by a three-night fast alone.
If one who is eating should experience purgation, he should recite [the Gāyatrī] three hundred times while unwell;
if well, three thousand times—the Gāyatrī is the supreme purification.

If a twice-born man is touched by Caṇḍālas or Śvapacas, or if excrement or urine has been voided [upon him], he should observe a three-night penance; however, if he has eaten while remaining impure from food remnants, he should perform it for six nights.
If an outcaste should touch a woman in her courses or a woman who has recently given birth, purification shall occur after three nights; thus Śātātapa declared.
But a menstruating woman who has been touched by dogs, elephants, crows, or the like, shall remain pure while fasting; she becomes purified by bathing at the [proper] time.
When two women who are menstruating should happen to touch one another anywhere,
they are purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and by the Brahmakūrca rite.
If a woman in her menses is ever touched by one who is impure from eating, she attains purification through a *kṛcchra* penance; a Śūdra woman, however, does so through giving gifts and fasting.
If one who is required to bathe when touched by what is impure from food (ucchiṣṭa) is instead touched by someone who is themselves impure from food,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
It is traditionally taught that for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse during the fertile period, bathing is prescribed due to the suspicion of pregnancy;
however, having approached a woman outside the fertile period, one should perform purification as required after voiding urine or feces.
Both husband and wife would be impure when they have gone to bed;
however, upon rising from the bed, the woman becomes pure while the man remains impure.
A woman who, out of wickedness, fails to attend to her husband’s body shall be fined twelve [paṇas] and, if she persists, shall be abandoned for one year without any provision for her maintenance.
Those who abandon non-outcast relatives shall be punished with the highest fine;
for while a father may indeed become an outcast by his own will, a mother can never do so.
He who attempts to kill himself by means such as ropes and the like, should, if dead, be smeared with impure substances; if he survives, the fine shall be two hundred [paṇas].
Their sons and friends shall each be fined one paṇa;
thereafter, they shall perform the penance as prescribed by the scriptures.

Those who have died by drowning or other forms of hanging, those who have fallen from the mendicant life or through fasting unto death, and those killed by poison, jumping from heights, ritual suicide, or weapons; (YS 99v.22)
These nine, having fallen from their status and being excluded by all the world,
are purified either by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance or by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
The sinner who has resorted to both [practices] and fallen from the dark and the speckled [stages] may be purified by two *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts, as well as by giving a cow and a bull.

If one is bitten by dogs, jackals, monkeys, and the like, or by humans, except during sexual intercourse, one becomes pure immediately after bathing; this applies whether it occurs during the day, at the twilights, or at night.
If a Brahmin ever eats the food of a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance,
he becomes pure after half a month by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel.
If a cow’s or a brahmin’s house has been burned, or if someone has died by hanging or similar means,
a twice-born man who cuts the ropes [of the corpse] should likewise perform one *kṛcchra* penance.
Having eaten the food of Caṇḍālas and Pukkāsas, or having gone to the wife of one [of these],
one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year if done knowingly, or two Aindava penances if done unknowingly.
Those who eat the food of Kāpālikas and likewise those who have sexual intercourse with their women should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year if done intentionally,
or two Cāndrāyaṇa penances if done unintentionally.
A Brahmin who has had sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, or who has consumed liquor or beef,
is purified by performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance followed by the *mauñjī-homa*.
Even all four who have committed great sins (mahāpātaka) without distinction are purified by entering the fire or by participating in a great sacrifice.
Likewise, by practicing even the concealment of secrets for a month,
a person standing within the water shall be purified by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
the fisherman, the Meda, and the Bhilla— these seven are recorded as the lowest castes (antyaja).
Having eaten from them, gone to their women, drunk their water, or accepted gifts from them,
one should perform a Kṛcchra penance for one year if done intentionally, or two Cāndrāyaṇas if done unintentionally.
Having approached his mother, the wife of his guru, his sister, his daughters, or his daughter-in-law, he shall enter the fire; no other purification is prescribed for him.
One should perform two *kṛcchra* penances for approaching a female renunciant of kings, or even one of the highest caste, as well as for approaching a woman of one's own lineage.
In the case of all other women who belong to a different paternal lineage (*pitṛgotra*) or even to a maternal lineage (*mātṛgotra*),
as well as in the case of all the wives of others, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance.
The twice-born remove the sin incurred by approaching a prostitute by drinking boiled water infused with *kuśa* grass for five nights, having done so once.
Some desire the vow for violating the teacher’s bed, some the vow for a slayer of a Brahmin, some that for a killer of a cow, and others that for one who has broken his vow of chastity.
But he who causes a cow to fall by striking it upward with a staff,
one should prescribe for him the double penance of the cow-vow.
But that which is as thick as a thumb, measuring one cubit in length,
moist, and covered with leaves, is proclaimed to be a "cow-staff" (godaṇḍa).
If, while killing cows, an embryo should also perish,
one must perform the Kṛcchra penance individually for each, just as was prescribed before.
If a foot has just emerged, or two feet have appeared, or the body is fully formed,
one declares that for killing an insentient fetus, the penance is three-quarters of a *kṛcchra*.
When the embryo is complete with all its major and minor limbs and endowed with semen, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for each [limb]; this is the expiation for a cow-killer.
If death occurs due to binding, confinement, a stone, or injury to cows,
the one who caused the circumstance is not tainted at all.
Whether swooning or even fallen, or likewise struck by a staff,
having risen, he shall go six steps, or seven, five, or even ten.
Whether one should take food or even drink water,
there is no penance for those whose previous diseases have been destroyed.
If cows are killed by wood, clods of earth, stones, or weapons,
how is the expiation prescribed in each respective scripture?
One should perform the Sāṃtapana penance for wood, the Prājāpatya for a clod of earth,
the Taptakṛcchra for a stone, and the Atikṛcchra for a weapon.
If misfortune should occur while one is giving medicine, oil, or food to cows or Brahmins,
no expiation is required.
In the drinking of oil as medicine, in the consumption of medicinal substances,
and likewise in the removal of a splinter, no penance is prescribed.
By tying a cord around the necks of calves, by means of ritual action, or by medicine—
for the sake of protection at night— there is no fault in confining or binding them.
If [the offense] is one-quarter, he should shave the hair on his feet; if it is one-half, only the beard;
if it is three-quarters, everything except the top-knot; but for a full offense, he should perform the rite at the root [of the lineage].
Having pulled out all the hair, one should cut it to a length of two finger-breadths;
for this indeed is the prescribed method for the shaving of the heads of women.
A woman should not perform the shaving of her head, nor likewise the vīrāsana posture;
she should not dwell in a cow-pen, nor should she follow after a man as he goes along.
Whether it be a king, a prince, or a learned Brahmin,
one should prescribe an expiation for them without having performed the shaving of the head.
And for the sake of preserving one's hair, one should prescribe a vow that is double [the standard duration];
when that double vow has been performed, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall likewise be double.
If even double the amount has not been given and one still protects one's hair,
the sin of the killer is not diminished, and the giver shall go to hell.
The king should punish with a fine those who prescribe expiatory rites not ordained by the Śruti or the Smṛti, as they are creators of obstacles to Dharma.
If the king, deluded by passion, should somehow fail to punish them,
that sin becomes tenfold and creeps back upon him alone.
Once the penance has been performed, he should then provide a feast for Brahmins and give them twenty cows along with a bull as a sacrificial fee.
If one is afflicted by worms born from a wound or by flies that have fallen upon it,
one should perform half of a *kṛcchra* penance and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability.
Having performed the expiation and having fed the best of the twice-born, one should give a māṣaka of gold; thereafter, purification is ordained.
If one is touched by Caṇḍālas or Śvapacas at night, bathing is prescribed;
however, one should not remain there for the night, as purification occurs immediately through bathing.
But if an unwise person should happen to stay there at night through ignorance,
then that sin of his is multiplied a hundredfold.
For when the stars rise, and likewise those planets that are above,
if one's rays are touched by them, one should perform a bath in water.

Clay should not be taken from within a wall, from water, from an anthill, from a mouse-hill, from a path, from a cremation ground, or from what remains after cleaning; these are the seven [prohibited types].
A Brahmin should diligently perform both *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and works of public utility);
through *iṣṭa* one attains heaven, and through *pūrta* one enjoys liberation.
That which is performed with a view toward wealth is called *iṣṭa*; a reservoir is called *pūrta*, as are especially groves and likewise temples for the gods.
He who rescues from ruin ponds, wells, tanks, and temples of the deities enjoys the fruit of meritorious works (pūrta).
One should take the urine of a white cow, likewise the dung of a black cow;
the milk of a copper-colored cow is to be taken, and curd is said to be from a white cow.
Clarified butter from a tawny cow should be taken, which destroys great sins;
likewise, at all sacred fords, one should offer substances individually with kusha grass into the water of a river.
Having taken it up with the *praṇava* alone, having raised it with the *praṇava*,
having stirred it together with the *praṇava*, one should drink it with the *praṇava*.
One should drink [the medicine] from a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree, or from a vessel made of copper,
or from a lotus leaf, or from a beautiful copper or earthen vessel.
But when birth-impurity has arisen and a second [impurity] occurs, there is no fault in the second; one is purified by the first alone.
That which is born is purified by [the birth of] another born, and likewise that which is dead by [the death of] another dead;
in the case of a miscarriage, one should prescribe three days [of impurity] for each month [of gestation].
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of gestation;
once her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who has become menstruating is purified by bathing.
A woman falls from her own lineage at the seventh step of the marriage ceremony;
her funeral rites, including the offering of rice balls and water, must be performed by the lineage of her husband.
There should be two rice-balls for the father; on each rice-ball, the names of two [ancestors] should be mentioned.
Three rice-balls should be offered for six [generations]; thus the giver does not become confused.
Having partaken of the *śrāddha* meal together with her own husband, the mother [is honored] along with the deity;
likewise, the grandmother and the great-grandmother [are honored] each with their own respective husbands.
Year after year, one should perform the honoring of one's mother and father;
one should offer a śrāddha without [invoking] the gods and present a single funeral cake (piṇḍa).
The wise should know that the śrāddha is of five kinds: the daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), the śrāddha for prosperity (vṛddhiśrāddha), and the pārvaṇa.

During an eclipse of a planet, at the transition of the sun (saṃkrānti), on festival days, and during the Mahālaya rites, a man should offer three pindas; however, on the anniversary of the day of death, he should offer only one.
An unmarried daughter is not separate from [her father's] funeral oblation and lineage during a period of birth-impurity;
she falls from her own lineage only through the mantras of the marriage ceremony.
By whichever caste a girl is married,
the impurity (sūtaka) pertaining to that [caste] applies to her, as does the offering of funeral cakes and water.
Once the marriage has been performed, on the fourth night,
she attains oneness with her husband in respect of the funeral cake, the lineage, and the birth-impurity.
On the first day, or the second, or the third, or the fourth,
the collection of the bones should be performed by relatives who have a mind intent on what is beneficial.
The collection of bones is prescribed for the castes in due order on the fourth, the fifth, the seventh, and likewise the ninth day.
On the eleventh day after the death of one for whom a bull is released,
he is liberated from the world of the departed spirits and is glorified in the heavenly world.
For that person of auspicious deeds whose bones float upon the waters of the Gaṅgā,
there is no return from the world of Brahmā by any means whatsoever.
As long as the bones of humans remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years they are honored in the heavenly world.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should contemplate with the heart:
"May my ancestors come; may they accept these handfuls of water."
Having joined the two hands well together and filled them with water,
one should draw up water to the depth of a cow's horn and pour it back into the midst of the water.
Standing in water and facing south, one should cast water into the sky;
for the sky is the station of the ancestors, as is the southern direction.
The waters are declared to be the host of gods, and likewise the waters are the host of ancestors;
therefore, one who desires the welfare of the ancestors should offer water into the waters.
Water is always pure: when heated by the rays of the sun during the day, by the stars and breezes at night, and by both during the two twilights.
Water that is naturally endowed with its own essence, never pervaded by impurity,
and whether contained in a vessel or resting on the ground, is always pure and sanctifying.
One should offer handfuls of water for the deities and the ancestors in the water;
one should offer handfuls of water for those who have died without funeral rites on dry land.
At a Śrāddha ceremony and at the time of the fire-oblation, one should give with a single hand;
at the libation of water (tarpaṇa), one should give with both hands—thus the Dharma is established.
Thus ends the Dharmaśāstra composed by Yama.
This *Yamasmṛti* is completed.
